title: Balancing your plate for steady blood sugar
body:
Managing blood sugar starts with how you fill your plate, not with giving up the foods you love.

## The plate method

Divide your plate into three sections:

- **Half the plate**: non-starchy vegetables like sukuma wiki, cabbage, spinach, or managu
- **A quarter of the plate**: protein such as beans, lentils, fish, or a small piece of chicken
- **A quarter of the plate**: starchy foods like a fist-sized portion of ugali, rice, or sweet potato

## Why portions matter more than elimination

Your body still needs carbohydrates for energy. The goal is to eat them in amounts your body can process without causing a sharp blood sugar spike. A fist-sized serving of ugali with a generous pile of sukuma wiki and beans is far better than a large ugali serving on its own.

## Practical tips for this week

1. At your next meal, try the plate method. No special ingredients needed.
2. Eat your vegetables and protein **before** the starchy portion. This slows sugar absorption.
3. If you feel hungry after eating, add more vegetables, not more ugali.

Small changes in portions make a real difference over time. You do not need to buy special food or follow a complicated diet.

title: Myth: Natural remedies can replace diabetes medication
body:
You may have heard that certain herbs, teas, or supplements can cure diabetes. This is one of the most dangerous myths about the condition.

## What the evidence says

There is **no proven herbal cure** for type 2 diabetes. Some natural substances like bitter melon (karela), cinnamon, and moringa have shown small effects on blood sugar in studies, but:

- The effects are **too small** to control diabetes on their own
- They have **not been tested** for safety when combined with diabetes medication
- Some herbal products **interact dangerously** with Metformin and other prescribed drugs
- The dosage in commercial products is **inconsistent** and unregulated

## The real danger

People who stop their prescribed medication in favour of herbal remedies risk:

- **Dangerously high blood sugar** (hyperglycaemia)
- **Kidney damage** that may not be reversible
- **Nerve damage** leading to numbness in feet and hands
- **Vision loss** from retinal damage

## What you can do

- **Never stop** your prescribed medication without talking to your doctor
- If you want to try a supplement, **tell your pharmacist first** so they can check for interactions
- Be sceptical of anyone selling a "cure" for diabetes. If it sounds too good to be true, it is.

Your medication is working even when you feel fine. That is the point.

title: The emotional weight of managing diabetes every day
body:
Living with diabetes is not just a physical challenge. The daily routine of medication, food choices, and worry takes a real emotional toll that many people never talk about.

## What diabetes burnout feels like

You might recognise some of these feelings:

- **Exhaustion** from thinking about food, medication, and blood sugar constantly
- **Guilt** when you eat something you think you should not have
- **Frustration** when your blood sugar readings do not make sense despite doing everything right
- **Loneliness** because people around you do not understand what it takes
- **Fear** about complications or the cost of treatment

If you feel any of these, you are not alone. Research shows that people with diabetes are **two to three times** more likely to experience depression.

## What helps

1. **Talk to someone you trust.** A friend, family member, or your pharmacist. Holding everything inside makes it heavier.
2. **Give yourself permission to have bad days.** Missing a dose or eating something off-plan does not erase all your good days.
3. **Focus on one thing at a time.** You do not need to be perfect at everything. Just take today's medication. That is enough for today.
4. **Connect with others in your situation.** Jireh Circles let you share experiences with people who genuinely understand.

## A reminder

You are doing something difficult every single day. The fact that you are reading this means you are still in the fight. That matters more than any single blood sugar reading.

title: Tracking your blood sugar: when, how, and what the numbers mean
body:
Checking your blood sugar at home gives you and your doctor valuable information about how well your treatment is working. Here is a practical guide to get the most from your readings.

## When to check

If you have a glucometer, the two most useful times to check are:

1. **Fasting (first thing in the morning before eating)**: This shows your baseline blood sugar level
2. **Two hours after your largest meal**: This shows how your body handles food

## What the numbers mean

| Reading | Target range | What it means |
|---------|-------------|---------------|
| Fasting | 4-7 mmol/L (72-126 mg/dL) | Your baseline is well controlled |
| After meals | Below 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) | Your body is processing food well |
| Below 4 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) | Too low (hypoglycaemia) | Eat something sugary immediately |
| Above 15 mmol/L (270 mg/dL) | Too high | Contact your doctor if persistent |

## How to make your readings useful

- **Write down every reading** in a notebook or on your phone. Include the date, time, and whether you had eaten.
- **Look for patterns**, not individual numbers. A single high reading is not a crisis. Three high fasting readings in a row is a pattern worth discussing with your doctor.
- **Bring your log to every doctor visit.** It helps them make better decisions about your medication.

## If you do not have a glucometer

Glucometers cost between KES 1,500-3,000 and test strips cost KES 25-50 each. Ask your pharmacist about affordable options. Even checking twice a week is better than not checking at all.

## Warning signs to watch for

- Fasting readings consistently above 10 mmol/L
- Frequent readings below 4 mmol/L (this may mean your medication dose needs adjusting)
- Sudden changes in your usual pattern

Tracking is not about achieving perfect numbers. It is about understanding your body and catching problems early.
